children.text: In the previous chapter, we considered symbolizing fairly basic English sentences with sentence letters of TFL. This leaves us wanting to deal with the English expressions ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘not’, and so forth. These are
connectives

—they can be used to form new sentences out of old ones. In TFL, we will make use of logical connectives to build complex sentences from atomic components. There are five logical connectives in TFL. This table summarizes them, and they are explained throughout this section.

These are not the only connectives of English of interest. Others are, e.g., ‘unless’, ‘neither … nor …’, and ‘because’. We will see that the first two can be expressed by the connectives we will discuss, while the last cannot. ‘Because’, in contrast to the others, is not
truth functional

If we let the TFL-sentence ‘

Conjunction
Consider these sentences:
Adam is athletic.
Barbara is athletic.
Adam is athletic, and also Barbara is athletic.
We will need separate sentence letters of TFL to symbolize

Adam is athletic.
Barbara is athletic.

children.text: Sentence 11

’. Thus we will symbolize it as ‘

conjunction
. We also say that ‘

conjuncts
of the conjunction ‘
Notice that we make no attempt to symbolize the word ‘also’ in

children.label: and3
children.text: sentence 11

. Words like ‘both’ and ‘also’ function to draw our attention to the fact that two things are being conjoined. Maybe they affect the emphasis of a sentence, but we will not (and cannot) symbolize such things in TFL.
Some more examples will bring out this point:
Barbara is athletic and energetic.
Barbara and Adam are both athletic.
Although Barbara is energetic, she is not athletic.
Adam is athletic, but Barbara is more athletic than him.

children.label: and4
children.text: Sentence 12
is obviously a conjunction. The sentence says two things (about Barbara). In English, it is permissible to refer to Barbara only once. It
might
be tempting to think that we need to symbolize

children.label: and4
children.text: sentence 12
with something along the lines of ‘
and energetic’. This would be a mistake. Once we symbolize part of a sentence as ‘
’, any further structure is lost, as ‘
’ is a sentence letter of TFL. Conversely, ‘energetic’ is not an English sentence at all. What we are aiming for is something like ‘
and Barbara is energetic’. So we need to add another sentence letter to the symbolization key. Let ‘
’ symbolize ‘Barbara is energetic’. Now the entire sentence can be symbolized as ‘

children.label: and5
children.text: Sentence 13

says one thing about two different subjects. It says of both Barbara and Adam that they are athletic, even though in English we use the word ‘athletic’ only once. The sentence can be paraphrased as ‘Barbara is athletic, and Adam is athletic’. We can symbolize this in TFL as ‘
’, using the same symbolization key that we have been using.

children.label: and6
children.text: Sentence 14

is slightly more complicated. The word ‘although’ sets up a contrast between the first part of the sentence and the second part. Nevertheless, the sentence tells us both that Barbara is energetic and that she is not athletic. In order to make each of the conjuncts a sentence letter, we need to replace ‘she’ with ‘Barbara’. So we can rewrite

children.label: and6
children.text: sentence 14

Both

Barbara is not athletic’. The second conjunct contains a negation, so we paraphrase further: ‘
Both

children.label: and6
children.text: sentence 14
and ‘Both Barbara is energetic and it is not the case that Barbara is athletic’. TFL does not (and cannot) preserve these nuances.

children.label: and7
children.text: Sentence 15

Both
Adam is athletic,
and
Barbara is more athletic than Adam’. (Notice that we once again replace the pronoun ‘him’ with ‘Adam’.) How should we deal with the second conjunct? We already have the sentence letter ‘
’, which is being used to symbolize ‘Adam is athletic’, and the sentence ‘

’ which is being used to symbolize ‘Barbara is athletic’; but neither of these concerns their relative athleticity. So, to symbolize the entire sentence, we need a new sentence letter. Let the TFL sentence ‘

A sentence can be symbolized as
if it can be paraphrased in English as ‘Both…, and…’, or as ‘…, but …’, or as ‘although …, …’.
We noted above that the contrast suggested by ‘but’ cannot be captured in TFL, and that we simply ignore it. A phenomenon that cannot simply be ignored is temporal order. E.g., consider:
Harry stood up and objected to the proposal.
Harry objected to the proposal and stood up.
If Harry stood up
after
he objected,

children.label: stoodsecond
children.text: sentence 17
is true but

children.label: stoodfirst
children.text: sentence 16
is false—the use of ‘and’ here is
asymmetric
. The symbol ‘
’ of TFL, however, is always symmetric (or “commutative” as logicians say). TFL cannot deal with asymmetric ‘and’. We’ll assume for all our examples and exercises that ‘and’ is symmetric.
On symmetric and asymmetric conjunction in linguistics, see, e.g., Robin Lakoff, “If’s, and’s, and but’s about conjunction”, in: C. J. Fillmore and D. T. Langendoen (eds.),
Studies in Linguistic Semantics
,  Holt, Rinehart & Winston, 1971, and Susan Schmerling, “Asymmetric conjunction and rules of conversation”, in: P. Cole and J. L. Morgan (eds.),
Speech Acts
You might be wondering why we put brackets around the conjunctions. The reason can be brought out by thinking about how negation interacts with conjunction. Consider:
It’s not the case that you will get both soup and salad.
You will not get soup but you will get salad.

children.label: negcon1
children.text: Sentence 18
can be paraphrased as ‘It is not the case that: both you will get soup and you will get salad’. Using this symbolization key:
You will get soup.
You will get salad.
we would symbolize ‘both you will get soup and you will get salad’ as ‘
’. To symbolize

children.label: negcon1
children.text: sentence 18
, then, we simply negate the whole sentence, thus: ‘

children.label: negcon2
children.text: Sentence 19
is a conjunction: you
will not
get soup, and you
will
get salad. ‘You will not get soup’ is symbolized by ‘
’. So to symbolize

children.label: negcon2
children.text: sentence 19
itself, we offer ‘

These English sentences are very different, and their symbolizations differ accordingly. In one of them, the entire conjunction is negated. In the other, just one conjunct is negated. Brackets help us to keep track of things like the
scope
of the negation.
Disjunction
Consider these sentences:
Either Fatima will play videogames, or she will watch movies.
Either Fatima or Omar will play videogames.
For these sentences we can use this symbolization key:
Fatima will play videogames
Omar will play videogames
Fatima will watch movies
However, we will again need to introduce a new symbol.

children.label: or1
children.text: Sentence 20
is symbolized by ‘
’. The connective is called
disjunction
. We also say that ‘
’ and ‘
’ are the
disjuncts
of the disjunction ‘

children.label: or2
children.text: Sentence 21
is only slightly more complicated. There are two subjects, but the English sentence only gives the verb once. However, we can paraphrase

children.label: or2
children.text: sentence 21
as ‘Either Fatima will play videogames, or Omar will play videogames’. Now we can obviously symbolize it by ‘
’ again.
A sentence can be symbolized as
if it can be paraphrased in English as ‘Either…, or….’
Sometimes in English, the word ‘or’ is used in a way that excludes the possibility that both disjuncts are true. This is called an
exclusive or
. An
exclusive or
is clearly intended when it says, on a restaurant menu, ‘Entrees come with either soup or salad’: you may have soup; you may have salad; but, if you want
both
soup
and
salad, then you have to pay extra.
At other times, the word ‘or’ allows for the possibility that both disjuncts might be true. This is probably the case with

children.label: or2
children.text: sentence 21
, above. Fatima might play videogames alone, Omar might play videogames alone, or they might both play.

children.label: or2
children.text: Sentence 21
merely says that
at least
one of them plays videogames. This is an
inclusive or
. The TFL symbol ‘
’ always symbolizes an
inclusive or
It will also help to see how negation interacts with disjunction. Consider:
Either you will not get soup, or you will not get salad.
You will get neither soup nor salad.
You get either soup or salad, but not both.
Using the same symbolization key as before,

children.label: or3
children.text: sentence 22
can be paraphrased in this way: ‘
Either
it is not the case that you get soup,
or
it is not the case that you get salad’. To symbolize this in TFL, we need both disjunction and negation. ‘It is not the case that you get soup’ is symbolized by ‘
’. ‘It is not the case that you get salad’ is symbolized by ‘
’. So

children.label: or3
children.text: sentence 22
itself is symbolized by ‘

children.label: or4
children.text: Sentence 23
also requires negation. It can be paraphrased as, ‘
It is not the case that:
either you get soup or you get salad’. Since this negates the entire disjunction, we symbolize

children.label: or4
children.text: sentence 23
with ‘

children.label: or.xor
children.text: Sentence 24
is an
exclusive or
. We can break the sentence into two parts. The first part says that you get one or the other. We symbolize this as ‘

’. The second part says that you do not get both. We can paraphrase this as: ‘It is not the case both that you get soup and that you get salad’. Using both negation and conjunction, we symbolize this with ‘
’. Now we just need to put the two parts together. As we saw above, ‘but’ can usually be symbolized with ‘
’. So

children.label: or.xor
children.text: sentence 24
can be symbolized as ‘
This last example shows something important. Although the TFL symbol ‘
’ always symbolizes
inclusive or
, we can symbolize an
exclusive or
in
TFL. We just have to use a few other symbols as well.
Conditional
Consider these sentences:
If Jean is in Paris, then Jean is in France.
Jean is in France only if Jean is in Paris.
Let’s use the following symbolization key:
Jean is in Paris
Jean is in France

children.label: if1
children.text: Sentence 25
is roughly of this form: ‘if
, then
’. We will use the symbol ‘
’ to symbolize this ‘if…, then…’ structure. So we symbolize

children.label: if1
children.text: sentence 25
by ‘
’. The connective is called the
conditional
. Here, ‘
’ is called the
antecedent
of the conditional ‘
’, and ‘
’ is called the
consequent

children.label: if2
children.text: Sentence 26
is also a conditional. Since the word ‘if’ appears in the second half of the sentence, it might be tempting to symbolize this in the same way as

children.label: if1
children.text: sentence 25
. That would be a mistake. Your knowledge of geography tells you that

children.label: if1
children.text: sentence 25
is unproblematically true: there is no way for Jean to be in Paris that doesn’t involve Jean being in France. But

children.label: if2
children.text: sentence 26
is not so straightforward: were Jean in Dieppe, Lyon, or Toulouse, Jean would be in France without being in Paris, thereby rendering

children.label: if2
children.text: sentence 26
false. Since geography alone dictates the truth of

children.label: if1
children.text: sentence 25
, whereas travel plans (say) are needed to know the truth of

children.label: if2
children.text: sentence 26
, they must mean different things.
In fact,

children.label: if2
children.text: sentence 26
can be paraphrased as ‘If Jean is in France, then Jean is in Paris’. So we can symbolize it by ‘
A sentence can be symbolized as
if it can be paraphrased in English as ‘If A, then B’ or ‘A only if B’.
In fact, the conditional can represent many English expressions. Consider:
For Jean to be in Paris, it is necessary that Jean be in France.
It is a necessary condition on Jean’s being in Paris that she be in France.
For Jean to be in France, it is sufficient that Jean be in Paris.
It is a sufficient condition on Jean’s being in France that she be in Paris.
If we think about it, all four of these sentences mean the same as ‘If Jean is in Paris, then Jean is in France’. So they can all be symbolized by ‘
It is important to bear in mind that the connective ‘
’ tells us only that, if the antecedent is true, then the consequent is true. It says nothing about a
causal
connection between two events (for example). In fact, we lose a huge amount when we use ‘
’ to symbolize English conditionals. We will return to this in

children.text: section 10.3
and

Biconditional
Consider these sentences:
Laika is a dog only if she is a mammal.
Laika is a dog if she is a mammal.
Laika is a dog if and only if she is a mammal.
We will use the following symbolization key:
Laika is a dog
Laika is a mammal
For reasons discussed above,

children.label: iff1
children.text: sentence 31
can be symbolized by ‘

children.label: iff3
children.text: Sentence 33
says something stronger than either

children.label: iff1
children.text: sentence 31
or

children.label: iff2
children.text: sentence 32
. It can be paraphrased as ‘Laika is a dog if Laika is a mammal, and Laika is a dog only if Laika is a mammal’. This is just the conjunction of

children.label: iff1
children.text: sentences 31 and 32
. So we can symbolize it as ‘
’. We call this a
biconditional
, because it amounts to stating both directions of the conditional.
We could treat every biconditional this way. So, just as we do not need a new TFL symbol to deal with
exclusive or
, we do not really need a new TFL symbol to deal with biconditionals. Because the biconditional occurs so often, however, we will use the symbol ‘
’ for it. We can then symbolize

children.label: iff3
children.text: sentence 33
with the TFL sentence ‘

The expression ‘if and only if’ occurs a lot especially in philosophy, mathematics, and logic. For brevity, we can abbreviate it with the snappier word ‘iff’. We will follow this practice. So ‘if’ with only
one
‘f’ is the English conditional. But ‘iff’ with
two
‘f’s is the English biconditional. Armed with this we can say:
A sentence can be symbolized as
if it can be paraphrased in English as ‘A iff B’; that is, as ‘A if and only if B’.

A word of caution. Ordinary speakers of English often use ‘if …, then…’ when they really mean to use something more like ‘…if and only if …’. Perhaps your parents told you, when you were a child: ‘if you don’t eat your greens, you won’t get any dessert’. Suppose you ate your greens, but that your parents refused to give you any dessert, on the grounds that they were only committed to the
conditional

(roughly ‘if you get dessert, then you will have eaten your greens’), rather than the biconditional (roughly, ‘you get dessert iff you eat your greens’). Well, a tantrum would rightly ensue. So, be aware of this when interpreting people; but in your own writing, make sure you use the biconditional iff you mean to.
Unless

We have now introduced all of the connectives of TFL. We can use them together to symbolize many kinds of sentences. An especially difficult case is when we use the English-language connective ‘unless’:
Unless you wear a jacket, you will catch a cold.
You will catch a cold unless you wear a jacket.
These two sentences are clearly equivalent. To symbolize them, we will use the symbolization key:
You will wear a jacket
You will catch a cold
Both sentences mean that if you do not wear a jacket, then you will catch a cold. With this in mind, we might symbolize them as ‘
Equally, both sentences mean that if you do not catch a cold, then you must have worn a jacket. With this in mind, we might symbolize them as ‘
Equally, both sentences mean that either you will wear a jacket or you will catch a cold. With this in mind, we might symbolize them as ‘
All three are correct symbolizations. Indeed, in

children.label: s:SemanticConcepts
children.text: chapter 12
we will see that all three symbolizations are equivalent in TFL.
If a sentence can be paraphrased as ‘Unless
,’ then it can be symbolized as ‘
’ or ‘

Again, though, there is a little complication. ‘Unless’ can be symbolized as a conditional; but as we said above, people often use the conditional (on its own) when they mean to use the biconditional. Equally, ‘unless’ can be symbolized as a disjunction; but there are two kinds of disjunction (exclusive and inclusive). So it will not surprise you to discover that ordinary speakers of English often use ‘unless’ to mean something more like the biconditional, or like exclusive disjunction. Suppose someone says: ‘I will go running unless it rains’. They probably mean something like ‘I will go running iff it does not rain’ (i.e., the biconditional), or ‘either I will go running or it will rain, but not both’ (i.e., exclusive disjunction). Again: be aware of this when interpreting what other people have said, but be precise in your writing.
